records.title: Termites
records.summary: Termites are very common on laterite. They mostly eat dead plant material, but in dry soil they attack seedlings, stems, pods and young trees.
instructions: Keep plenty of mulch and crop residue on the soil: termites prefer it to living plants.
Keep seedlings moist; termite damage is worst in dry spells.
Remove and destroy badly attacked plants; re-sow gaps.
Keep mulch a hand's width from young tree stems.
limitations: Termites also break down mulch and improve the soil; do not try to wipe them out.
Poisoning mounds is harmful and has a poor record.
safety_notes: Never use unlabelled or improvised chemical poisons.
Keep any spray away from drinking water, children and animals.
signs: Seedlings wilting and snapping at the base

bio_options.preparation: No preparation: pick pests off by hand or knock them into a container of soapy water.
safe_use: Do it early morning when insects are slow.
Check under leaves and inside flowers.
cautions: Some caterpillars and beetles (such as blister beetles) irritate skin: use a leaf or cloth, not bare fingers.

records.title: Grasshoppers and crickets
records.summary: Grasshoppers chew leaves and can strip seedlings, especially at the start of the rains and near dry grassland.
instructions: Hand-pick or knock into soapy water in the cool morning.
Re-sow badly damaged spots with reserved seed.
Keep chickens, if any, working the plot edges.
limitations: Swarms of locusts are beyond what a plot can manage; protect seed and re-sow later.
safety_notes: Never use unlabelled or improvised chemical poisons.
Keep any spray away from drinking water, children and animals.
signs: Ragged holes and chewed leaf edges
Many hoppers jumping as you walk

bio_options.name: Neem leaf or seed extract
bio_options.preparation: Crush a few handfuls of fresh neem leaves or dried, shelled neem seeds, soak overnight in a bucket of clean water, strain through cloth, and add a little plain soap so it sticks. Use the same day.
safe_use: Spray or splash onto leaves in the late afternoon, covering undersides.
Test on a few plants first and wait a day for leaf damage before treating more.
Repeat only if pests return, about a week later.
Wash hands, face and tools afterwards.
cautions: Neem is not harmless: keep it out of eyes and mouth, and away from drinking water.
Do not spray on open flowers when bees are active.
Use only on pests that are clearly building up, not as routine.
Strength varies a lot with seed age and preparation; old seed is weak.
Do not store the extract; it loses strength quickly.

records.summary: Small soft insects clustering on shoots, flowers and young pods, often in dry spells.
instructions: Rub clusters off by hand or wash with a splash of plain water.
Pinch off the worst affected tips.
Ladybirds and other predators often arrive; avoid killing them.
limitations: Do not spray when bees are visiting flowers.
safety_notes: Never use unlabelled or improvised chemical poisons.
Keep any spray away from drinking water, children and animals.

Remove and destroy badly bored pods.
Harvest dry pods promptly.
limitations: Neem works best on young caterpillars; large ones must be picked.
safety_notes: Never use unlabelled or improvised chemical poisons.

records.title: Striga (witchweed)
records.summary: A parasitic weed that attaches to millet (and a related one to cowpea) roots, stunting the crop. It has bright pink, purple or white flowers.
instructions: Pull striga carefully by hand before it flowers or as soon as flowers appear, without breaking the stem.
Carry pulled plants out of the field in a bag; do not leave them lying, as seed can still ripen.
Burn or bury them deeply far from the plot.
Keep pulling all season and after harvest; seed lasts in soil for many years.
Rotate or mix millet with cowpea or horse gram, and add compost or manure, which reduces striga over time.
limitations: One season of pulling is not enough; stopping lets the seed bank rebuild.
safety_notes: Never use unlabelled or improvised chemical poisons.
Keep any spray away from drinking water, children and animals.
signs: Small upright plants with bright pink-purple flowers growing among millet
Millet stunted and yellow with no other cause

records.title: Stored grain and pulse weevils
records.summary: Small beetles that breed inside stored grain and pulses, leaving holes and powder.
instructions: Dry grain fully before storing (it should crack when bitten).
Store in clean, tightly closed containers; seal well so insects cannot breathe and multiply.
Mix stored pulses with a little clean, sieved wood ash or dry neem leaves (traditional practice).
Check every week or two; sun-dry and re-clean infested lots.
limitations: Never mix chemical pesticides into food grain.
safety_notes: Never use unlabelled or improvised chemical poisons.
Keep any spray away from drinking water, children and animals.

bio_options.preparation: Dry clean neem leaves in shade and layer a handful in the container.
safe_use: Remove leaves and wash grain before cooking.
cautions: Traditional practice; strength varies.

records.title: Leaf spots, blast and mould
records.summary: Fungal diseases cause spots, streaks or mould on leaves and heads, worst in warm, humid, crowded conditions.
instructions: Thin plants so air moves between them.
Remove badly affected leaves or plants and take them away from the plot.
Do not save seed from diseased plants.
Rotate crops between seasons.
limitations: There is no reliable home cure; prevention and clean seed matter most.
safety_notes: Never use unlabelled or improvised chemical poisons.
Keep any spray away from drinking water, children and animals.

Eye-shaped spots on finger millet leaves and necks (blast)

records.title: Birds on ripening heads
records.summary: Birds can take much of a millet crop in the last weeks before harvest.
instructions: Scare birds in the early morning and evening, when they feed most.
Hang strips of cloth or shiny material on sticks; move them often.
Cover the best heads with cloth or old sacks once grains fill.
Harvest promptly once grain is hard.
Lay thorny branches over low heads or ripening pods.
Use nets or cloth bags over the best heads where available.
limitations: Birds get used to fixed scarers; change them often.
safety_notes: Never use unlabelled or improvised chemical poisons.
Keep any spray away from drinking water, children and animals.

records.title: Tree pests to watch (cashew and mango)
records.summary: Young trees can be hit by termites, stem borers and sucking bugs on new shoots and flowers.
instructions: Inspect young trees weekly in the first years.
Cut out and destroy dried shoots.
Keep the base clean and mulch away from the trunk.
Seek local advice early if borers are found.
limitations: Large trees are hard to treat; prevention and early checks matter.
safety_notes: Never use unlabelled or improvised chemical poisons.
Keep any spray away from drinking water, children and animals.
signs: Gum or sawdust oozing from the trunk (borers)

records.summary: Caterpillars chew holes in tender leaves of greens and moringa, especially in the early rains.
instructions: Check both sides of leaves every few days and hand-pick caterpillars in the cool morning.
Remove badly eaten leaves.
Pick greens often so few old leaves remain.
limitations: Sprays are a last resort on leaves you will eat; wash leaves well and keep any spray off food close to picking.

records.title: Sweet potato weevil
records.summary: Small weevils enter through cracks in the mound and tunnel into roots, making them bitter.
instructions: Pile soil over cracks in the mound as roots swell.
Plant clean cuttings from vine tips.
Harvest on time; do not leave roots long in dry, cracked soil.
Rotate: do not plant sweet potato in the same bed next season.
limitations: There is no simple home cure once roots are tunnelled; prevention is what works.
safety_notes: Never use unlabelled or improvised chemical poisons.
Keep any spray away from drinking water, children and animals.

records.title: Cassava mosaic disease
records.summary: A virus spread by whiteflies and infected cuttings that mottles and twists cassava leaves and stunts roots.
instructions: Plant cuttings only from healthy, unmottled plants.
Pull out and remove infected plants early, away from the plot.
Watch for whiteflies with a sticky yellow trap.
safety_notes: Never use unlabelled or improvised chemical poisons.
Keep any spray away from drinking water, children and animals.

instructions: Store grain and pulses in sealed pots or tins raised off the ground on stones or a platform.
Keep stores and the area around them clean of spilled grain.
Keep thick mulch and brush piles away from stores.
Use simple traps where locally safe, away from children and pets.
